'''Anne Lucy Bosworth Focke''' (September 29, 1868 – May 15, 1907) was an American mathematician who became the first mathematics professor at what is now the [[University of Rhode Island]], and later became the first female doctoral student of [[David Hilbert]].

==Early life==
Bosworth was originally from [[Woonsocket, Rhode Island]].{{r|bw|mt}} When she was four, her father and a younger sister died, and she grew up in a family of women: her mother (a librarian), her grandmother (also widowed), and her aunt.{{r|mt}}

==Undergraduate education and academic work==
Bosworth attended [[Woonsocket High School]],{{r|mt}} and graduated from [[Wellesley College]] in 1890.{{r|bw|mt|pw}} At Wellesley, her classmates included mathematicians [[Grace Andrews (mathematician)|Grace Andrews]] and [[Clara Latimer Bacon]].{{r|pw}}

She worked for two years as a teacher at [[Amesbury High School]] in Massachusetts, and was appointed as an instructor of mathematics at the Rhode Island College of Agriculture and Mechanic Arts (later to become the [[University of Rhode Island]]) in early 1892, the first year the school became a college. One month later she became its professor of mathematics and physics.{{r|bw|mt|pw}}

==Graduate education==
While continuing to work at the college, Bosworth earned a [[master's degree]] at the [[University of Chicago]] from 1894 through 1896 through summer study with [[E. H. Moore]] and [[Oskar Bolza]].{{r|bw|mt|pw}}

In 1898, taking a leave from her work for the college, Bosworth traveled to the [[University of Göttingen]] in Germany, where she worked under the supervision of [[David Hilbert]]. She defended her dissertation there in 1899, and was awarded the [[Thesis|Ph.D]]. in 1900.<ref>Chronology from Green and LaDuke and MacTutor. Wyant gives slightly different dates.</ref> Her dissertation was ''Begründung einer vom Parallelenaxiome unabhängigen Streckenrechnung'',{{r|mg}} and concerned [[non-Euclidean geometry]].{{r|mt}} She was David Hilbert's first female doctoral student,{{r|bw}} part of a group that later included [[Nadeschda Gernet]] (1902), [[Vera Myller]] (1906), [[Margarete Kahn]] (1909), [[Klara Löbenstein]] (1910), and Eva Koehler (1912).{{r|mg}}

==Later life==
In 1901 Bosworth married Theodore Moses Focke, an American civil engineer, [[Materials science|materials scientist]], and applied mathematician whom she had met in Göttingen.{{r|mt|pw}} Soon afterwards she followed her husband to [[Cleveland, Ohio]], leaving her academic work (except for assisting her husband in grading) to raise a family of three children. She caught [[pneumonia]] in 1907 and died of it.{{r|bw}}
